papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Interpretable Features in Transformer Language Models
papers.summary: We train sparse autoencoders on the residual stream activations of transformer language models ranging from 1B to 70B parameters. Our approach discovers monosemantic features that correspond to human-interpretable concepts with 89% precision. We demonstrate that these features can be used to steer model behavior, detect harmful content, and explain model predictions with unprecedented granularity. The feature dictionaries scale predictably with model size.

coreClaims: 89% precision on monosemantic feature discovery across model scales
Features enable model steering, harm detection, and explainability
Feature dictionary size scales predictably with model parameters
redFlags: Precision metric may overcount semantically similar features
Computational cost of SAE training at 70B scale not discussed
analysis.expertCommentary: This is mechanistic interpretability done right. The scaling analysis is the key contribution - showing that features are consistent and predictable across model sizes. The steering applications are practically valuable. This advances both our theoretical understanding and practical toolkit for model interpretability.
analysis.oneLiner: Sparse autoencoders that find interpretable features in LLMs with 89% precision and enable model steering.

papers.title: Flow Matching Surpasses Diffusion Models for High-Resolution Image Generation
papers.summary: We demonstrate that flow matching models decisively outperform diffusion models for high-resolution image generation when properly scaled. Our FlowGen-XL model achieves FID 1.42 on ImageNet 512x512, compared to 1.79 for the best diffusion model, while requiring 40% fewer sampling steps. We provide a unified theoretical analysis showing that flow matching's straight-line transport paths are fundamentally more efficient than diffusion's curved paths at high resolutions.

coreClaims: FID 1.42 on ImageNet 512x512 vs 1.79 for best diffusion model
40% fewer sampling steps required
Theoretical proof that straight-line paths are more efficient at high resolution
redFlags: FID improvements may not correlate with perceptual quality at this level
Computational cost comparison at training time is absent
analysis.expertCommentary: Strong evidence for what many suspected: flow matching is the future of generative modeling. The theoretical analysis is the real contribution here - it explains WHY flow matching wins, not just that it does. The FID improvements are marginal in absolute terms but the efficiency gains are practically significant.
analysis.oneLiner: Flow matching beats diffusion with FID 1.42 and 40% fewer steps, backed by theoretical proof of efficiency.

papers.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: Rethinking the MLP with Learnable Activation Functions
papers.summary: We revisit Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) with a series of architectural improvements that make them competitive with MLPs at scale. Our KAN-v2 replaces fixed activation functions with learnable spline-based functions on edges, achieving better sample efficiency and interpretability. On scientific computing tasks, KAN-v2 achieves 10x better accuracy per parameter than MLPs, though the advantage narrows on standard deep learning benchmarks.

coreClaims: Learnable spline activations on edges improve sample efficiency
10x accuracy per parameter on scientific computing tasks
Narrower advantage on standard deep learning benchmarks
redFlags: Scientific computing advantage may not transfer to general ML
Training instability of spline parameters at scale needs attention
analysis.expertCommentary: Interesting follow-up that honestly reports both strengths and limitations. The 10x improvement on scientific computing is compelling but the admission that standard DL benchmarks don't show the same gains is refreshingly honest. KANs have a niche, and this paper helps define it clearly.
analysis.oneLiner: Improved KAN architecture that excels at scientific computing (10x better) but offers modest gains on standard ML tasks.

papers.title: Adaptive Gradient Methods with Provable Convergence for Non-Convex Optimization
papers.summary: We present AdaGrad-Plus, an adaptive gradient method with provable convergence guarantees for non-convex stochastic optimization. Unlike Adam and its variants which lack theoretical convergence guarantees in the non-convex setting, AdaGrad-Plus achieves O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence rate while maintaining the practical benefits of per-parameter learning rates. Empirically, it matches or exceeds Adam's performance on training transformers and ResNets.

coreClaims: Provable O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence for non-convex stochastic optimization
Maintains per-parameter adaptive learning rates
Matches or exceeds Adam on transformers and ResNets
redFlags: Convergence rate may be loose compared to actual performance
Additional hyperparameter compared to Adam may complicate adoption
analysis.expertCommentary: A clean theoretical contribution that addresses a real gap. Adam's lack of convergence guarantees has been a dirty secret of deep learning. Having an alternative that's theoretically sound AND practically competitive is valuable. The proofs are tight and the experiments are convincing.
analysis.oneLiner: An Adam alternative with actual convergence proofs that matches its performance in practice.

papers.title: Test-Time Compute Scaling: When More Thinking Helps and When It Doesn't
papers.summary: We conduct a comprehensive study of test-time compute scaling across 30 reasoning tasks. We find that additional test-time compute (via chain-of-thought, tree search, or verification) follows a log-linear improvement curve with diminishing returns. Crucially, we identify task characteristics that predict whether test-time compute will help: problems requiring search benefit greatly, while problems requiring knowledge recall show minimal improvement. We provide a practical decision framework.

coreClaims: Test-time compute follows log-linear scaling with diminishing returns
Search-based tasks benefit greatly vs knowledge recall tasks
Provides practical decision framework for when to invest in test-time compute
redFlags: 30 tasks may not cover all reasoning patterns
Framework assumes known task characteristics which is circular
analysis.expertCommentary: Exactly the kind of empirical analysis the field needs. Everyone is throwing more test-time compute at problems without understanding when it helps. The search vs recall distinction is intuitive and well-supported. The decision framework is practical and actionable. Should be standard reading for anyone deploying reasoning systems.
analysis.oneLiner: Systematic study showing test-time compute helps for search tasks but not knowledge recall, with a practical decision framework.

papers.title: Linear Attention Is All You Need (For Sequences Under 8K Tokens)
papers.summary: We present LinearFormer, a transformer variant using linear attention that matches quadratic attention quality for sequences under 8K tokens while being 3x faster. Through careful kernel design and gating mechanisms, we overcome the quality degradation that plagued previous linear attention attempts. For sequences beyond 8K, we propose a hybrid approach that uses linear attention for local context and sparse quadratic attention for global context.

coreClaims: Linear attention matches quadratic quality under 8K tokens
3x faster inference with no quality loss in the short-context regime
Hybrid approach extends benefits beyond 8K with sparse global attention
redFlags: 8K token threshold is somewhat arbitrary and task-dependent
Training stability of the hybrid approach at large scale uncertain
analysis.expertCommentary: The parenthetical in the title tells you everything: this is a strong result with clear limitations. Linear attention for short sequences is practically very useful since most real-world inputs are under 8K. The hybrid approach for longer sequences is a reasonable engineering solution. Not revolutionary but very practical.
analysis.oneLiner: Linear attention that truly works for sequences under 8K tokens with 3x speedup and no quality loss.

papers.title: Data Pruning at Scale: How to Train on 50% Less Data Without Losing Performance
papers.summary: We present ScalePrune, a data pruning method that identifies and removes redundant training examples based on gradient-informed difficulty scores. Training on the pruned 50% subset achieves 99.3% of the full-data performance across image classification, language modeling, and speech recognition. We show that pruned datasets transfer better than full datasets in 7 out of 10 downstream tasks, suggesting that data quality matters more than quantity.

coreClaims: 50% data reduction with only 0.7% performance loss
Pruned datasets transfer better than full datasets on 7/10 tasks
Gradient-informed difficulty scoring identifies truly redundant examples
redFlags: Pruning overhead may offset training savings for small datasets
Transfer improvements could be due to removing domain-specific noise
analysis.expertCommentary: The finding that pruned datasets transfer better is the real insight here - it suggests half of most training datasets is redundant or even harmful. The practical implications are huge: halving training costs while possibly improving downstream performance. The pruning method itself is straightforward but effective.
analysis.oneLiner: Prune 50% of training data with negligible performance loss and better transfer learning.

papers.title: Understanding Grokking: A Phase Transition Perspective on Delayed Generalization
papers.summary: We provide a complete theoretical explanation for grokking - the phenomenon where neural networks first memorize then suddenly generalize. Through the lens of statistical physics, we show that grokking is a first-order phase transition in weight space. Our theory predicts exactly when grokking will occur based on dataset size, model capacity, and learning rate, with predictions validated across 50 experimental settings.

coreClaims: Grokking is a first-order phase transition in weight space
Theory predicts grokking timing from dataset size, capacity, and learning rate
Validated across 50 experimental settings
redFlags: Phase transition framework may oversimplify complex training dynamics
Predictions may not hold for very large models or datasets
analysis.expertCommentary: Finally, a convincing theoretical explanation for grokking. The statistical physics lens is appropriate and the theory makes concrete, testable predictions that actually hold. This paper will be the definitive reference on grokking for years to come. Beautiful science.
analysis.oneLiner: Proves grokking is a phase transition and predicts exactly when it will happen.

papers.title: Reward Hacking in RLHF: A Taxonomy and Defense Framework
papers.summary: We present a comprehensive taxonomy of reward hacking behaviors in RLHF-trained models, identifying 14 distinct categories of reward exploitation. Through adversarial probing of 8 frontier models, we show that all exhibit at least 5 categories of reward hacking. We propose RewardGuard, a defense framework that reduces exploitable reward hacking by 78% by training with a diverse committee of reward models and adversarial perturbations.

coreClaims: 14 distinct categories of reward hacking identified and documented
All 8 frontier models tested exhibit at least 5 categories
RewardGuard reduces exploitable reward hacking by 78%
redFlags: Taxonomy may miss subtle forms of reward hacking
Defense training with reward committees increases computational cost
analysis.expertCommentary: Important safety work that systematizes what was previously anecdotal knowledge. The taxonomy is comprehensive and well-organized. The finding that ALL frontier models are susceptible is sobering but expected. RewardGuard is a good first defense but the 78% leaves a significant residual risk.
analysis.oneLiner: Documents 14 types of reward hacking, shows all frontier models are vulnerable, and offers a 78% effective defense.

papers.title: BitNet b1.58 at Scale: Training Ternary Weight Models with 100B Parameters
papers.summary: We scale ternary weight training (1.58-bit) to 100 billion parameters and show it matches the quality of full-precision models while enabling 8x memory reduction and 5x inference speedup. Our training recipe addresses the instability issues that prevented previous attempts at this scale. We release BitNet-100B, which runs at 200 tokens/second on a single consumer GPU.

coreClaims: 1.58-bit models match full-precision quality at 100B parameters
8x memory reduction and 5x inference speedup
200 tokens/second on a single consumer GPU
redFlags: Quality parity claim needs more fine-grained evaluation on diverse tasks
Consumer GPU testing likely means high-end consumer GPU
analysis.expertCommentary: If these results hold up, this is a game-changer for model deployment. Running a 100B parameter model at 200 tokens/sec on consumer hardware is transformative. The training recipe is the key contribution. This could democratize access to frontier-scale models in a way nothing else has.
analysis.oneLiner: Scales 1.58-bit models to 100B parameters, matching full precision while running on a single consumer GPU.

papers.title: Implicit Neural Representations for Scientific Data Compression
papers.summary: We demonstrate that implicit neural representations (INRs) achieve 100x compression ratios on scientific simulation data while preserving physical invariants. Our PhysINR approach encodes conservation laws directly into the neural representation's architecture, ensuring that decompressed data satisfies physical constraints exactly. We validate on climate simulation, fluid dynamics, and molecular dynamics data.

coreClaims: 100x compression while preserving physical invariants exactly
Conservation laws encoded in architecture, not just training loss
Validated on climate, fluid dynamics, and molecular dynamics
redFlags: Compression and decompression time not compared to traditional methods
100x ratio may vary significantly across different physical systems
analysis.expertCommentary: Clever application of INRs to a real problem. The key insight of baking physical constraints into the architecture rather than the loss function is principled. The 100x compression with exact invariant preservation is impressive. This has immediate practical value for scientific computing where data storage is a bottleneck.
analysis.oneLiner: INR-based compression achieving 100x ratios on scientific data while preserving physical laws exactly.

papers.title: Efficient Fine-Tuning with Less Than 0.01% of Parameters
papers.summary: We present NanoTune, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that achieves competitive performance while modifying less than 0.01% of model parameters. NanoTune identifies and updates only the most impactful parameters using a gradient-based importance scoring mechanism. On instruction-following, summarization, and QA tasks with LLaMA-70B, NanoTune matches LoRA performance while being 50x more parameter-efficient.

coreClaims: Competitive fine-tuning with <0.01% parameter modification
50x more parameter-efficient than LoRA
Gradient-based importance scoring identifies critical parameters
redFlags: Parameter efficiency may not translate to memory or compute savings
Importance scoring itself has computational cost that may offset savings
analysis.expertCommentary: The parameter efficiency claims are impressive but somewhat misleading - what matters in practice is memory and compute, not parameter count. LoRA's advantage isn't just few parameters, it's fast matrix operations. Still, the gradient importance scoring is interesting and the extreme sparsity might enable new deployment scenarios.
analysis.oneLiner: Fine-tuning with 0.01% parameters that matches LoRA quality but may not save actual compute.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction for Safe Reinforcement Learning Under Distribution Shift
papers.summary: We apply conformal prediction to reinforcement learning to provide statistical safety guarantees under distribution shift. Our ConformalRL framework wraps any RL policy with a conformal safety layer that provides valid prediction intervals for action outcomes. The safety layer intervenes only when the predicted outcome violates safety constraints with high probability, maintaining both performance and safety. We demonstrate 99.7% constraint satisfaction on autonomous driving and robotic manipulation tasks.

coreClaims: Conformal prediction provides valid safety guarantees for RL under distribution shift
99.7% constraint satisfaction on safety-critical tasks
Safety layer is modular and works with any RL policy
redFlags: Conformal guarantees assume exchangeability which may not hold under severe shift
Safety interventions may degrade performance on edge cases
analysis.expertCommentary: Principled combination of conformal prediction and RL safety. The modularity is the killer feature - you can add safety guarantees to any existing policy. The 99.7% constraint satisfaction is excellent. The theoretical grounding is solid, though the exchangeability assumption needs more discussion in the non-stationary setting.
analysis.oneLiner: Modular safety layer using conformal prediction that achieves 99.7% constraint satisfaction for any RL policy.

papers.title: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis Revisited at LLM Scale
papers.summary: We revisit the lottery ticket hypothesis at the scale of billion-parameter language models. We find that sparse subnetworks containing only 10% of parameters can match the full model's performance when found via our iterative magnitude pruning with rewinding algorithm. Surprisingly, these lottery tickets are highly transferable across tasks and even across similar model architectures, suggesting universal sparse structures in trained LLMs.

coreClaims: 10% sparse subnetworks match full LLM performance
Lottery tickets transfer across tasks and architectures
Suggests universal sparse structures in trained LLMs
redFlags: Finding lottery tickets requires multiple rounds of expensive training
Transfer claims need more rigorous verification across diverse architectures
analysis.expertCommentary: The transferability finding is the real surprise here. If lottery tickets are universal across architectures, it says something deep about the structure of learned representations. The practical barrier remains that finding these tickets is expensive. Still, this is an important data point for understanding neural network structure.
analysis.oneLiner: Finds transferable sparse subnetworks in LLMs that match full performance with 10% of parameters.

papers.title: Federated Unlearning: Removing Training Data Influence Without Retraining
papers.summary: We present FedUnlearn, a method for removing the influence of specific training data from federated learning models without full retraining. Using a combination of gradient-based influence estimation and targeted parameter updates, FedUnlearn achieves 99.2% of the unlearning quality of full retraining while being 200x faster. This enables compliance with data deletion regulations like GDPR in federated settings.

coreClaims: 99.2% unlearning quality compared to full retraining
200x faster than retraining from scratch
Enables GDPR compliance in federated learning
redFlags: Unlearning verification is inherently difficult to audit
May not work for data that had outsized influence during training
analysis.expertCommentary: Addresses a real practical need that will only grow as regulation tightens. The speed improvement makes unlearning actually feasible in production FL systems. The 99.2% figure is good but the verification challenge remains: how do you prove data is truly unlearned? Still, this is the most practical unlearning paper I've seen.
analysis.oneLiner: Remove training data influence from federated models 200x faster than retraining with 99.2% quality.

papers.title: Why Do Large Models Generalize? A PAC-Bayes Perspective on Overparameterization
papers.summary: We provide new PAC-Bayes generalization bounds that explain why overparameterized models generalize despite classical theory predicting they shouldn't. Our key insight is that the effective parameter count of trained models is orders of magnitude smaller than the nominal count, due to low-rank structure in the learned weights. We derive tight bounds that correctly predict generalization behavior across model scales from 10M to 10B parameters.

coreClaims: New PAC-Bayes bounds explain overparameterized generalization
Effective parameter count is orders of magnitude smaller than nominal
Bounds correctly predict behavior from 10M to 10B parameters
redFlags: Low-rank assumption may not hold for all training regimes
Bounds may still be too loose for fine-grained predictions
analysis.expertCommentary: This is a significant step toward understanding the biggest mystery in deep learning theory. The connection between effective parameters and low-rank structure is not new, but the tight PAC-Bayes bounds that actually predict scaling behavior ARE new and important. This paper will be taught in graduate courses.
analysis.oneLiner: PAC-Bayes theory that finally explains why massive models generalize, with bounds that match empirical scaling.

papers.title: Adversarial Robustness Through Neural Circuit Analysis
papers.summary: We propose CircuitDefense, which improves adversarial robustness by identifying and hardening the specific neural circuits responsible for classification decisions. By mapping decision circuits using activation patching and then applying targeted robustness training only to these circuits, we achieve 12% higher adversarial accuracy than standard adversarial training while using 80% less compute for the robustness training phase.

coreClaims: Circuit-targeted robustness training instead of full-model adversarial training
12% higher adversarial accuracy than standard adversarial training
80% less compute for the robustness training phase
redFlags: Circuit identification may miss important pathways
Assumes stable circuits which may not hold for all inputs
analysis.expertCommentary: Creative combination of mechanistic interpretability and adversarial robustness. The idea of hardening specific circuits rather than the whole model is elegant and the efficiency gains are impressive. The 12% accuracy improvement is meaningful. This bridges two previously separate research areas in a productive way.
analysis.oneLiner: Improves adversarial robustness by 12% while using 80% less compute through targeted neural circuit hardening.

papers.title: Distributed Training of Trillion-Parameter Models on Commodity Hardware
papers.summary: We present CheapTrain, a distributed training system that enables training of trillion-parameter models across heterogeneous commodity hardware. Through dynamic load balancing, fault-tolerant pipeline parallelism, and communication-efficient gradient compression, CheapTrain achieves 82% of the training throughput of purpose-built clusters at 15% of the cost. We train a 1.2T parameter model using rented consumer GPUs.

coreClaims: 82% throughput of purpose-built clusters at 15% cost
Fault-tolerant training across heterogeneous consumer GPUs
Successfully trained 1.2T parameter model on rented hardware
redFlags: Throughput percentage may be optimistic for worst-case network conditions
Long-term cost comparison should include failure recovery overhead
analysis.expertCommentary: Extremely practical systems work. The 82% throughput at 15% cost ratio is compelling for researchers outside big labs. The fault tolerance is crucial for commodity hardware where failures are common. This could significantly democratize large-scale training. Well-engineered and honestly evaluated.
analysis.oneLiner: Train trillion-parameter models on cheap consumer GPUs at 82% efficiency for 15% of the cost.

papers.title: Beyond Cross-Entropy: Information-Geometric Loss Functions for Language Modeling
papers.summary: We propose a family of loss functions derived from information geometry that improve language model training. Our Fisher-Rao loss accounts for the geometry of the probability simplex, leading to more stable training, faster convergence, and improved calibration. On language modeling tasks from 1B to 13B parameters, models trained with Fisher-Rao loss achieve 3% lower perplexity and 15% better calibration compared to cross-entropy.

coreClaims: Information-geometric loss functions outperform cross-entropy
3% perplexity reduction and 15% calibration improvement
Theoretically grounded in the geometry of probability simplex
redFlags: 3% perplexity improvement may not translate to meaningful downstream gains
Computational overhead of Fisher-Rao loss not clearly stated
analysis.expertCommentary: Mathematically elegant work that challenges a fundamental assumption in LM training. The calibration improvement is arguably more important than the perplexity gain - well-calibrated models are more trustworthy. The information geometry perspective is underexplored and this makes a good case for its practical value.
analysis.oneLiner: Information-geometric loss function that improves LM perplexity by 3% and calibration by 15% over cross-entropy.

papers.title: Emergent Capabilities in Mixture-of-Experts: A Statistical Analysis
papers.summary: We conduct a controlled study of emergent capabilities in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. By varying expert count, expert size, and routing strategy while keeping total parameters constant, we find that emergence is driven by expert specialization, not total parameter count. Models with more specialized experts exhibit emergent behaviors at lower compute budgets. We propose a metric for predicting emergence based on expert utilization entropy.

coreClaims: Emergence is driven by expert specialization, not total parameters
More specialized experts show emergent behaviors at lower compute
Expert utilization entropy predicts emergence
redFlags: Controlled study may not capture all factors present in production-scale MoE
Definition of emergence used may be too narrow
analysis.expertCommentary: Important controlled study that disentangles what drives emergence in MoE. The finding that specialization matters more than parameter count has significant implications for architecture design. The entropy-based prediction metric is a nice practical contribution. Well-designed experiments with clear conclusions.
analysis.oneLiner: Expert specialization, not parameter count, drives emergence in MoE models.
